subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on the periodic table, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain the periodic table for GCSE simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Arrangement of the Periodic Table: groups, periods and proton number order
Group I alkali metals: properties and trends in reactivity
Group VII halogens: properties, trends and displacement reactions
Group VIII/0 noble gases and their inertness
Transition elements: properties, catalysts, coloured compounds and variable oxidation states
Trends in metallic and non-metallic character

questions.lo: Arrangement of the Periodic Table: groups, periods and proton number order
questions.q: In the modern Periodic Table, elements are arranged in order of increasing what?
questions.explain: Elements are arranged in order of increasing proton number (atomic number).

questions.lo: Arrangement of the Periodic Table: groups, periods and proton number order
questions.q: What is a vertical column of elements in the Periodic Table called?
questions.explain: Vertical columns are groups; horizontal rows are periods.

questions.lo: Arrangement of the Periodic Table: groups, periods and proton number order
questions.q: An element is in Group IV and Period 3. How many electrons are in its outer shell and how many shells does it have?
questions.explain: The group number gives the number of outer-shell electrons (4), and the period number gives the number of occupied electron shells (3).

questions.lo: Arrangement of the Periodic Table: groups, periods and proton number order
questions.q: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical properties?
options: They have the same number of outer-shell electrons
They have the same number of neutrons
They have the same relative atomic mass
questions.explain: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell (valence) electrons, which determines their chemical properties.

questions.lo: Group I alkali metals: properties and trends in reactivity
questions.q: Which of these is a physical property of the Group I alkali metals?
options: They do not react with water
They are relatively soft and can be cut with a knife
They have very high melting points
questions.explain: Alkali metals are relatively soft (they can be cut with a knife) and have low densities compared with most metals.

questions.lo: Group I alkali metals: properties and trends in reactivity
questions.q: Going DOWN Group I from lithium to potassium, how does reactivity change?
questions.explain: Reactivity increases down Group I: the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost, so the metal reacts more vigorously.

questions.lo: Group I alkali metals: properties and trends in reactivity
questions.q: When potassium reacts with water, which products form?
questions.explain: Alkali metals react with water to form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas: potassium + water gives potassium hydroxide + hydrogen.

questions.lo: Group I alkali metals: properties and trends in reactivity
questions.q: Going down Group I, melting point and density change how?
options: Melting point decreases and density generally increases
Melting point increases and density decreases
questions.explain: Down Group I the melting point decreases while the density generally increases.

questions.lo: Group VII halogens: properties, trends and displacement reactions
questions.q: At room temperature, what is the physical state and colour of chlorine?
questions.explain: Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas. Bromine is a red-brown liquid and iodine is a grey-black solid at room temperature.

questions.lo: Group VII halogens: properties, trends and displacement reactions
questions.q: Going DOWN Group VII from chlorine to iodine, how does reactivity change?
questions.explain: Reactivity decreases down Group VII: the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so it is harder to gain an electron.

questions.lo: Group VII halogens: properties, trends and displacement reactions
questions.q: Chlorine is added to potassium bromide solution. What happens?
options: Chlorine displaces bromine, turning the solution orange
No reaction because chlorine is less reactive
questions.explain: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from potassium bromide, forming potassium chloride and bromine (orange).

questions.lo: Group VII halogens: properties, trends and displacement reactions
questions.q: Going down Group VII, how do the melting and boiling points change?
questions.explain: Melting and boiling points increase down Group VII, which is why chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature.

questions.lo: Group VIII/0 noble gases and their inertness
questions.q: Why are the noble gases (Group VIII/0) very unreactive (inert)?
options: They have a full outer electron shell
They have only one outer electron
questions.explain: Noble gases have a full (stable) outer electron shell, so they have little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons and are chemically inert.

questions.lo: Group VIII/0 noble gases and their inertness
questions.q: Which use of a noble gas relies on it being unreactive?
options: Argon used to fill filament light bulbs
questions.explain: Argon is used in filament lamps because it is inert and will not react with the hot filament, preventing it from burning away.

questions.lo: Transition elements: properties, catalysts, coloured compounds and variable oxidation states
questions.q: Which is a typical property of the transition elements?
options: They are very soft and float on water
Low melting points and low density
questions.explain: Transition elements form coloured compounds. They also have high melting points and high density, act as catalysts and show variable oxidation states.

questions.lo: Transition elements: properties, catalysts, coloured compounds and variable oxidation states
questions.q: Iron can form Fe2+ and Fe3+ ions. This illustrates which transition-element property?
questions.explain: Forming ions with different charges (Fe2+ and Fe3+) shows that transition elements have variable oxidation states.

questions.lo: Transition elements: properties, catalysts, coloured compounds and variable oxidation states
questions.q: Which transition element or compound is used as a catalyst in the Haber process?
questions.explain: Iron is used as the catalyst in the Haber process. Many transition elements and their compounds act as catalysts.

questions.lo: Transition elements: properties, catalysts, coloured compounds and variable oxidation states
questions.q: Compared with Group I metals, transition metals are generally:
options: Lower melting and coloured only as gases
questions.explain: Transition metals are harder, denser and have higher melting points than Group I metals, and are generally much less reactive.

questions.lo: Trends in metallic and non-metallic character
questions.q: Across a period from left to right, how does metallic character change?
questions.explain: Across a period, elements change from metals to non-metals, so metallic character decreases and non-metallic character increases from left to right.

questions.lo: Trends in metallic and non-metallic character
questions.q: Where in the Periodic Table are the most metallic elements found?
options: In the middle transition block only
Top right and top left equally
questions.explain: Metallic character increases down a group and decreases across a period, so the most metallic elements are found towards the bottom left of the Periodic Table.
